briefs.summary: Two stresses got worse this week. Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia hit the main Hormuz bypass, and Brent rose 6% to US$116.72, its highest settle since April. Asian LNG went above US$30. Meanwhile the AI funding worry spread from the neoclouds to the hyperscalers: Meta raised its capex floor but posted its first negative free cash flow since 2012, and chips had their worst day since June (SOX −6.7% on 22 Oct). Money moved into Treasuries (the 10y briefly closed below 5%) and staples. The costs are building underneath, though: P&G raised its commodity hit to US$1.4bn, and a December Fed hike is still about 78% priced. In SG, core inflation undershot at 2.0%, REITs bounced off their lows, and Cat B COE rose to S$131,901 as buyers rushed EV purchases ahead of the incentive cut. MSFT, GOOGL and AMZN (28–29 Oct), the FOMC (28 Oct) and the oil majors (29–30 Oct) are all in the coming week.

sections.headline: Meta raises its capex floor but posts its first cash burn since 2012; chips post their worst day since June and the hyperscaler verdict moves to 28–29 Oct

what_happened.text: Meta Q3 2026 (21 Oct): revenue US$64.6bn against US$63.31bn expected. EPS was US$3.83 against 6.67 expected, after a US$9.89bn legal charge (US$7.40 excluding it). The 2026 capex range was narrowed to US$135–145bn from US$130–145bn, which raises the floor. The Q4 revenue guide is US$73–76bn. No 2027 capex number was given; Meta said budgets are 'still in development' and it will keep investing aggressively.

Meta's Q3 free cash flow was −US$2.12bn, its first negative quarter since 2012. Capex including finance leases was US$34.9bn against US$32.8bn of operating cash flow. Meta also announced a new listed non-voting Class C share, to be paid as a one-for-one stock dividend effective 19 Jan 2027.

Thu 22 Oct: META −7.0% to US$648.85, Philadelphia Semiconductor Index −6.7% (worst day since 23 Jun), Nasdaq Composite −2.60% to 26,008.86, S&P 500 −1.21%. AMD, Intel, Sandisk and Marvell each fell more than 8%. CoreWeave fell about 10% on renewed cost-of-capital worries.
Lam Research, September quarter (21 Oct): revenue US$8.22bn (+22% q/q), GAAP operating margin 40.0%, December-quarter guide US$8.6bn ± US$0.4bn. The stock still fell 11.8% on 22 Oct.

Tesla Q3 2026 (21 Oct): revenue US$28.0bn, adjusted EPS US$0.48, quarterly capex US$4.7bn (+110% y/y). Prior 2026 guide was more than US$25bn, framed around 'superintelligence compute' and chip manufacturing. TSLA fell 3.1% on 22 Oct as investors weighed heavier 2027–28 spending plans.

CoreWeave hit a 2026 intraday low of US$59.31 on 19 Oct and closed at US$61.12, the same day Goldman upgraded it. Total debt is about US$52bn; its 9.75% 2031 bond yields 15.7%. Five-year CDS reached a record 1,194.5bp in the prior week.
Median on-demand H100 rental price, week of 19 Oct: US$3.71/GPU-hr across 40 providers, up about 10% over 4 weeks and about 25% over 12 months.
Coming up: Microsoft FQ1 2027 on Wed 28 Oct after the close; Alphabet Q3 on Wed 28 Oct (call 4:30pm ET); Amazon Q3 on Thu 29 Oct (call 5pm ET); Intel Q3 on Thu 29 Oct after the close.

sections.first_order: Demand-side data stayed firm. Meta raised its capex floor, Lam guided higher at a record margin, and GPU rental prices kept rising. The market sold the funding side instead: the first hyperscaler to report showed capex now exceeds operating cash flow and added a new equity class. Chips had their worst day since June, and CoreWeave fell again. The question has moved from 'is there demand' to 'can even the hyperscalers fund it from cash flow'. This week's losses were milder than last week's, but SMH, NVDA and QQQ all closed the week lower.

second_order.effect: With Meta's free cash flow negative, more capex has to come from debt or equity. That makes funding language in the 28–29 Oct calls as important as the capex numbers.
A fresh ~10% drop in CoreWeave and bond yields near 15–16% keep its cost of capital punitive. If hyperscalers start leaning on external funding, the market for weaker borrowers gets more crowded.

second_order.sector: Semicap and SG suppliers (LRCX, AMAT; UMS, AEM, Frencken)
second_order.effect: Lam's record 40% margin and higher December guide point to continued tool orders. Lam's large Singapore manufacturing base and local precision-parts suppliers benefit from the volume. The 11.8% fall in Lam's shares shows that sentiment, not orders, is setting prices for now.
H100 median up about 10% in 4 weeks, so compute is still scarce and the costs of AI startups and app developers keep rising.

second_order.sector: Rate-sensitive tech and DC REITs (incl. Keppel DC REIT, Digital Core REIT)
second_order.effect: The US 10-year fell about 19bp to 4.95% on 22 Oct in a flight to safety, which eases discount rates and refinancing costs for data-centre landlords. Tenant credit risk at the neoclouds is still the offset.

Against: CoreWeave about −10% on 22 Oct; 9.75% 2031 bond at 15.7% yield; debt about US$52bn

sections.headline: STI dips below its 9 Oct low intraday on 23 Oct but closes flat on the week; REITs bounce 3% off 52-week lows ahead of the 29 Oct updates

what_happened.text: STI closed 5,422.16 on Fri 23 Oct, +6.63 pts (+0.12%) w/w. Closing high 5,437.99 (Wed 21 Oct), closing low 5,404.02 (Tue 20 Oct). Banks rallied on Wed (OCBC +1.2%, UOB +1.4%, DBS +0.3%) and fell on Tue, Thu and Fri.

23 Oct: STI touched 5,365.33 intraday, below the 9 Oct low of 5,369.49, then closed +0.13% as the AI/semis selloff eased. DBS −0.2% to S$74.44, OCBC −0.2% to S$29.00, UOB −0.7% to S$41.59. Market is waiting for the Fed on 28 Oct.

Keppel DC REIT, the first S-REIT to report Q3: 9M DPU 8.57 Scts vs 7.67 a year earlier, distributable income S$228m vs S$195.3m. Units +~4% on 23 Oct. CapitaLand China Trust 9M gross revenue fell to RMB1.22bn from 1.28bn, yet units rose ~1%.

23 Oct closes: CICT S$2.30 (+2.2% on the day; 52w range 2.20–2.57), CLAR S$2.23 (+1.8%; 52w 2.14–2.91), Parkway Life REIT S$4.07 (52w 3.91–4.31). None of the three filed an announcement this week. CICT and CLAR 3Q updates are still due 29 Oct.

sections.first_order: A flat index hid a rotation. Banks drifted into their results (DBS 5 Nov, OCBC 6 Nov) and finished the week roughly unchanged. REITs bounced off their 52-week lows (CICT +3.1% w/w, CLAR +2.8%) on a strong first Q3 print (Keppel DC REIT) and a softer core CPI, which helps the lower-for-longer SG rates case. The 23 Oct intraday break below the 9 Oct low was bought back, so that support held on a closing basis but has been tested.

second_order.effect: Keppel DC REIT's 9M DPU +11.7% sets a high bar. If the 29 Oct CICT/CLAR updates show positive rental reversions and stable cost of debt with the SGS 10y at 2.34%, the bounce off the 2.20/2.14 lows has fundamental backing. If they don't, it fades.
September core CPI at 2.0% (below the 2.3% consensus) lowers the odds of further MAS tightening, which keeps SORA and SGD-asset yields soft and weighs on Q3/Q4 NIM going into 5–6 Nov results
Turnover eased (S$1.8bn value on a day this week vs September's S$1.92bn DAV), so the volatility-driven volume tailwind is fading as the selloff calms
Bank shares are flat and still ~6–8% below their September highs, so household portfolios are not rising. That is neutral to a mild drag on Cat B bids, and so far it is not visible in COE bidding.

sections.headline: Cat B COE rises 1.4% to S$131,901 as the Car Expo and the end of the EV incentive pull demand forward; Cat A tops Cat B again

what_happened.text: 2nd October 2026 exercise (closed 21 Oct): Cat A S$132,004 (+2,003; 1,574 bids / 1,191 quota), Cat B S$131,901 (+1,801; 1,149 bids / 923 quota), Cat C S$92,200 (+311; 481/308), Cat D S$10,778 (−234; 611/539), Cat E S$135,790 (−1,210; 411/270). PQP: Cat A S$129,883, Cat B S$131,819. Cat A is the second-highest on record (record S$133,009 on 9 Sep).

Motorist gives Cat C as S$92,900 in its body text and table. LTA's own release was not fetched, so treat Cat C as unconfirmed between 92,200 and 92,900. Cat A closed above Cat B for the fourth time this year.

LTA urged buyers and dealers to bid prudently ahead of the Car Expo (24–25 Oct). The EV Early Adoption Incentive (45% of ARF, cap S$7,500) ends for EVs registered from 1 Jan 2027, cutting the maximum EV ARF saving from S$30,000 to S$20,000. Remaining 2026 rounds: 2–4 Nov, 16–18 Nov, 7–9 Dec, 21–23 Dec. LTA is quoted as saying 'We expect a short-term increase in COE prices' (secondary source).

LTA consultation (opened 8 Oct, closes 11:59pm 2 Nov): merge Cat A and B into one car category with an OMV-based feebate. In the 3-band option, the bottom 35% by median OMV get a S$15,000 rebate and models above the 50th percentile pay a S$15,000 surcharge. The 5-band option uses ±S$7,500/±S$15,000 steps. Options for Cat E are to remove it or restrict it to cars. Findings due H1 2027; this is not yet policy.

LTA also flagged online initial bids, a review of bidding fees and dealer pricing shown ex-COE. It rejected pay-as-you-bid because ~3 in 4 successful 2025 Cat A/B bids were within 5% of the clearing price.
No Nov 2026–Jan 2027 quota announcement found as of 25 Oct. The last one was the LTA Aug–Oct 2026 release.
September CPI: private transport inflation slowed to 7.1% y/y from 7.5% as car price increases moderated.

sections.first_order: Bullish here means premiums rising. Cat B bids exceeded quota by 24% (1,149 vs 923), and two demand pulls (the Car Expo, and EV buyers needing 2026 registration to keep the S$7,500 EEAI) point to firm or higher premiums through the four remaining 2026 rounds. The 3-month check (25 Jan 2027) lands after that deadline, though. The January 2027 rounds lose the EV pull-forward, and the Nov–Jan quota, still unannounced, is the main swing factor. Near-term pressure is up; the window to check_on is two-sided.

second_order.effect: The registration-date cut-off for the EEAI concentrates EV orders into Nov–Dec 2026 and creates an order air-pocket in Q1 2027

A S$15,000 surcharge above the 50th OMV percentile, if adopted after H1 2027, raises the cost of premium cars relative to mass-market ones. Buyers may bring forward purchases before any change, which supports Cat B bids now.
COE rises of ~1.4% per round keep private transport inflation elevated (7.1%) even as car list-price increases slow. Private transport sits in headline CPI, not core.
Premiums above S$130K plus loan-to-value caps raise the down-payment needed, which caps loan volumes even as ticket sizes stay high
Removing or restricting Cat E would end its use as a Cat B overflow channel; Cat E S$135,790 is still the highest premium of all categories

evidence: Cat B S$131,901, +1.38% vs S$130,100 at last brief; bids/quota 1.24x
Cat A S$132,004, within S$1,005 of its 9 Sep record; Cat A has exceeded Cat B in four rounds this year
EEAI ends for EVs registered from 1 Jan 2027, so EV demand is time-boxed into the four remaining 2026 rounds

Dealers and commentators link the Cat A/B convergence to EVs engineered to fit Cat A power limits, which is LTA's stated rationale for the merger
Opposition MP Jamus Lim welcomed the merger proposal as similar to his 2025 proposal (political reaction only)
sections.flip_if: Bullish (premiums rising) if the Nov–Jan quota cuts Cat B certificates per round below ~923, or the 2–4 Nov round clears above S$135,001 with bids/quota above ~1.3x. Bearish (premiums falling) if the quota rises materially, Cat B bids/quota falls toward 1.1x after the Car Expo, January 2027 rounds show a post-EEAI drop, or LTA signals early implementation of a surcharge on high-OMV cars. Toward the S$80K thesis: needs a quota jump plus a demand shock (retrenchments, MAS tightening, dealer pullback).

sections.headline: Brent jumps 6% to US$116.72, highest since late April, as Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia join the Hormuz attacks; talks stall

what_happened.text: Brent settled US$116.72 on Fri 23 Oct (+US$3.55 on the day, about +6% w/w, highest settle since 29 Apr); WTI US$103.27 (+3.8% on the day, +2.3% w/w). It traded around US$108–111 on 20–22 Oct before the Saudi strikes.

The Houthis hit Saudi targets, including energy infrastructure, an oil field and an airport. Aramco told staff to leave its Dhahran HQ. The US ordered non-emergency personnel out of Saudi Arabia. No lost Saudi barrels reported; Aramco says the East-West line is at its 7m b/d maximum.

Iran's IRGC claimed seven tankers hit in or near Hormuz (unverified by AP; Trump called it fabricated). UKMTO logged 32 attacks around the Arabian Peninsula in October so far, against 16 in all of September. Flow data conflict: Kpler via Bloomberg has Gulf crude flows at 24.6m b/d in the week to 18 Oct (Vortexa 18m), while IMF PortWatch logged only 4 Hormuz transits on 18 Oct against a pre-crisis 85 a day.

US–Iran: no formal talks. Iran's FM Araqchi says he has 'no trust whatsoever' in US peace aims; President Pezeshkian says talks cannot proceed while the US blockade stays. Markets are pricing possible renewed US strikes before the 3 Nov midterms.
EIA, week to 16 Oct: commercial crude −3.1mb to 412.5mb (about 3% below the 5-yr average); gasoline −3.0mb (5% below); distillates +1.7mb to 104.3mb (9% below); SPR 282.7mb; refinery runs 93.4%.

Stock releases are small so far. DOE authorised an SPR exchange of only up to 400k bbl for Phillips 66 Lake Charles; the SPR is at its lowest since 1982. Germany's EBV made the first G7-agreed release. The US eased some Russia sanctions in exchange for more Russian diesel: 2.3mb this month, possibly 7.6mb a month later.

Asian spot LNG topped US$30/MMBtu on 20 Oct, the first time since Dec 2022, after a tanker strike in the Gulf of Aden. North Asia spot was US$29.30 in the week to 16 Oct, against US$10.40 at end-February. EU storage is 74.6% full against a ~89% seasonal norm. Qatar told buyers its force majeure runs through November, and Edison's Italian cargoes are suspended to early December.
OPEC+ (7 members) held November quotas flat at 31.01m b/d on 4 Oct; it meets next on 1 Nov. The quotas are mostly moot: Saudi output was about 8m b/d in September against a 10.478m quota.
Majors' Q3 dates: Shell 29 Oct (07:00 GMT); ExxonMobil 30 Oct (05:30 CT); Chevron call 30 Oct (11:00 ET, secondary source); BP reportedly 30 Oct (secondary source, not confirmed by BP).
XLE closed US$69.33 on 23 Oct (+2.6% on the day), a new 52-week high (intraday US$69.72).

sections.first_order: The risk has spread from Hormuz to Saudi Arabia, the main bypass (East-West line to Yanbu, then past the Houthi-contested Bab al-Mandab), so the Hormuz premium now sits on top of a Saudi-infrastructure premium. Inventories are still drawing: US crude and gasoline fell, distillates are 9% below average and the SPR is at a 1982 low, so policy buffers are thin. Majors go into Q3 prints (29–30 Oct) with Brent about 6% higher than a week ago and refining margins already flagged as record. The offsets are real but smaller: Gulf flows may be recovering (Kpler), Russian diesel is coming via the sanctions waiver, and the US administration has a midterm incentive to push prices down.

second_order.effect: Jet fuel prices track gasoil, and distillates are tight (US stocks 9% below average). Brent at US$116 lifts SIA's unhedged fuel cost. Higher fuel surcharges, on top of SG's green jet-fuel levy on flights from 1 Oct, raise fares and soften price-sensitive leisure demand. Houthi strikes on a Saudi airport add to Middle East routing risk.

JKM above US$30 plus Brent-linked term LNG (Japan, and SG's Brent-indexed gas) feeds into Q1 2027 electricity tariffs in Japan, Korea and Singapore. Qatar's force majeure through November removes the winter relief valve.
Distillate stocks are 9% below the 5-yr average heading into winter, so diesel and fuel surcharges rise. Carriers pass most of it on with a lag, while shippers' (and staples') logistics costs go up.
Product inventories are tight, Kuwaiti fuel output is still impaired and Russian refineries are under drone attack, so cracks stay high. Russian diesel to the US is the main offset.
Energy-linked packaging, freight and refrigeration costs hit consumer-goods gross margins with a 1–2 quarter lag. This week's Brent jump extends the squeeze into Q1 2027 costs.
US gasoline stocks are 5% below average, so pump prices keep headline CPI elevated into the Fed decision. That keeps pressure on long-duration assets.

sections.headline: Fuel window for the Q1 2027 tariff now runs at Brent ~US$109–117 and LNG ~US$30; SG renews its Qatar LNG MOU and names three biomethane importers

what_happened.text: EDB appointed Keppel Energy, Sembcorp Utilities and Tuas Power as aggregators in a 15-year, 300MW biomethane import sandbox (23 Oct). First supply is due by end-2028, aimed at data centres and industry. DPM Gan Kim Yong announced it with S$143m for industrial decarbonisation.

Keppel's share is up to 120MW for 15 years, 'not expected to have a material impact' on current-year EPS. Its Connectivity arm was provisionally awarded 50MW of new data-centre capacity. The 3Q business update is on 29 Oct.

PM Wong and Qatar's Emir (19 Oct, Doha) welcomed renewal of the QatarEnergy–Singapore MOU on LNG and low-carbon tech 'to support stable LNG procurement'. No volumes or terms were disclosed. Qatar's force majeure still runs through November.
EMC/EMA data: monthly average USEP hit S$332.5/MWh in August 2026 (July 245.2, Feb 132.9), the latest month published. Wholesale power is far above the level implied by the Q4 household tariff cut.
Q4 2026 household tariff is 28.59 c/kWh (−10.4%). The Q1 2027 tariff is due around end-December. No new SP Group statement this week.
Sembcorp closed S$6.01 on 23 Oct (S$6.00 on 20 Oct; day range 5.88–6.04), up from S$5.93 at last brief. 52-week range S$5.22–7.20.

sections.first_order: The fuel-cost window for the Q1 2027 tariff (roughly October to mid-December forward prices) is running well above the window behind the Q4 cut: Brent US$109–117 and Asian LNG at US$29–30. A Q1 tariff increase is the likely direction; this is an inference, not an announcement. For Sembcorp and Keppel, high wholesale prices (USEP S$332/MWh in August) support merchant generation spreads, though gencos mostly pass fuel through on contracted volumes. The biomethane roles add future optionality only, with nothing material before 2028.

second_order.effect: A Q1 2027 tariff rise would reverse the Q4 cut and push electricity back up in headline and core CPI from January
Elevated USEP widens spreads on uncontracted capacity. Retail-arm margins get squeezed if fixed-price contracts were signed before the spike.
Power is their largest operating cost. Higher tariffs flow into lease renewals, and biomethane offtake adds a green premium option from 2028.
Higher electricity for refrigerated stores and diesel for logistics raises opex into H1 2027

sections.headline: P&G and Nestlé pass the volume test and hold guidance, but P&G raises its commodity cost hit to $1.4bn and loses 150bp of gross margin

what_happened.text: P&G FY27 Q1 (22 Oct): net sales +4% to $23.3bn and organic +4%, made up of volume +2.4%, mix +1.1% and price only +0.4%. Core EPS $2.00 (+1%). Core gross margin fell 150bp, with commodities costing 140bp, offset by 120bp of productivity savings and 20bp of pricing. Organic growth guidance (1–3%) and core EPS guidance ($6.89–7.11) held; all-in sales guidance raised to 2–4% to include the Thorne acquisition.

P&G raised its after-tax FY27 commodity cost estimate from about $1.0bn (29 Jul) to about $1.4bn and doubled its interest-cost estimate. Total headwinds are now $0.79 per share (was $0.56). The slides say cost headwinds will increase over the next few quarters.
PG rose about 6% intraday on 22 Oct, its biggest gain since 2020, as investors rotated from tech into defensives. It closed at 165.59, then fell back to 161.02 on 23 Oct.

Nestlé 9M (22 Oct): Q3 organic growth 4.0%, with real internal growth (RIG) 2.8% and pricing 1.1%; 9M organic 3.7% (RIG 1.9%, pricing 1.8%). FY26 outlook kept: 3–4% organic, a higher underlying trading operating margin, and an H2 margin broadly similar to H1. Coffee pricing continues to ease.
Unilever's Q3 trading statement is on 28 Oct, not this week. The next FAO Food Price Index is due 6 Nov; September stood at 136.0, the highest since Nov 2022.
XLP closed at 88.26 on 23 Oct (+3.31% on 22 Oct, −1.92% on 23 Oct), up 0.7% on the week. WMT closed at 119.89 (16 Oct: 118.81).

sections.first_order: The volume half of the test passed: P&G volume +2.4% and Nestlé Q3 RIG +2.8%, both with guidance held. The margin half failed: P&G's gross margin fell 150bp, its cost estimate rose 40%, and it captured only 0.4% of price. Branded makers are buying volume by not passing costs on, so earnings growth is flat (P&G core EPS +1%) even as sales grow. Haven flows from the AI selloff are lifting the sector's prices more than its fundamentals.

second_order.sector: Branded household and personal care (PG, CL, KMB)

what_happened.text: US September CPI +0.6% m/m, 3.7% y/y (consensus 3.6%); core 2.6% y/y (Aug 2.4%); gasoline +7.1%.
September PPI +1.3% m/m, 6.3% y/y; industrial production +0.7%.
Boston Fed's Collins: 'appropriate to raise rates a bit further before the end of the year'. Fed funds 3.75–4.00%; FOMC 27–28 Oct.
Initial jobless claims 199k (week to 10 Oct), continuing 1.71m: no recession signal in the labour market.
US 10y closed 5.08% on 16 Oct, down from 5.24% at the 9 Oct close; 2y 4.71%.

sections.first_order: Inflation data argue for more Fed hikes, but long bonds rallied as equity money sought safety during the chip selloff. TLT gained 2.6% against last week's bearish read. The 10y has not broken below 5.0%, so the higher-for-longer regime is intact.

second_order.effect: A Fed that keeps hiking into 3.7% CPI caps multiples even if the 10y dips on haven flows
Fed hike odds at 74% support the USD vs currencies whose central banks paused, such as SGD after MAS's hold
Real income squeeze from 3.7% CPI and US$100 WTI fuels trade-down to value retailers

evidence: CPI 3.7% beat consensus; PPI 6.3% y/y signals more pipeline inflation
CME December hike odds 74.3%, up from 50.2% a month earlier
Claims at 199k: the labour market gives the Fed room to hike
Against: 10y fell 16bp on the week and TLT rose 2.6% to 80.05
consensus: The Fed hikes again in December; October is a live meeting
Haven demand for Treasuries rises when the AI-credit story wobbles
sections.flip_if: A 10y close below 5.0% that holds after the 27–28 Oct FOMC, an FOMC statement that signals a pause, a weak October payrolls print, or Brent falling below US$100 would flip this to bullish for bonds.

sections.headline: MAS holds instead of tightening a third time; GDP slows to 5.4% and SGS yields drop

what_happened.text: MAS kept the S$NEER slope, width and centre unchanged on 14 Oct; the band 'will allow S$NEER to continue to strengthen'. 2027 core and headline inflation forecast 1.5–2.5%.
Q3 advance GDP +5.4% y/y (Q2 6.2%); manufacturing slowed to 7.5% from 12.9%.
OCBC: S$NEER about 1.65% above the policy midpoint after the decision, down from 1.85%; USD/SGD range 1.2760–1.2840.
SGS 10y yield 2.34% on 16 Oct vs 2.45% at the last brief.

sections.first_order: Last week's base case (a third tightening) was wrong: MAS paused, which is dovish relative to expectations. The SGD gave back a little of its premium and local yields fell. Growth is still solid but cooling.

second_order.effect: Lower SGS yields and no extra SGD tightening ease financing costs
A slower SGD appreciation path passes more of the oil and food price rise into CPI
A paused S$NEER slope eases competitiveness pressure while NODX runs hot on AI hardware

evidence: MAS hold vs a market expecting tightening (MAS statement)
SGS 10y −11bp to 2.34%
Q3 GDP 5.4%, manufacturing growth roughly halved
USD/SGD ~1.281 (15 Oct), little changed from 1.2793
consensus: MAS stays on hold in January unless core inflation rises above 2.5%
OCBC sees USD/SGD upside risk toward 1.28–1.29
sections.flip_if: September CPI (~23 Oct) with core above 2.5% would revive tightening odds (bullish SGD). A sharp drop in Q3 retrenchments data or NODX would turn the read bearish on SG growth.

briefs.summary: One root cause runs through the week: US long yields at their highest since 2002 (10y closed at 5.31% on 5 Oct) on top of Brent back above US$106 from Hormuz tanker attacks. The FOMC minutes show most officials want another hike, and MAS is expected to tighten again on 14 Oct. That combination triggered a bank-led 4.1% STI drop (worst day since April 2025) and pushed SG REITs to 52-week lows. It also re-ignited input-cost inflation for staples, where PepsiCo cut EPS guidance. Refiners are the clear winners: Shell's margin is up from US$24 to US$42/bbl. AI hardware demand (TSMC, Samsung) still beats forecasts despite the OpenAI revenue reset.

sections.headline: Chip orders still beating forecasts while the OpenAI revenue reset raises doubts about end-demand

what_happened.text: TSMC Q3 2026 revenue was NT$1.49tn, a record. It was up 17.6% q/q and beat the top of guidance. September sales were NT$511.9bn, +54.6% y/y.
Samsung's Q3 preliminary operating profit was KRW107.4tn (+782% y/y), above consensus. Tight DRAM supply and HBM4 shipments for Nvidia's Vera Rubin drove it.
The FT reported OpenAI's annualised revenue at about US$50bn, not the ~US$70bn cited earlier, mostly because of how revenue is counted. On 8 Oct ORCL, AMD and NVDA fell 3–5% intraday.
Broadcom is in early talks to arrange more than US$50bn of financing for OpenAI's custom chips (WSJ/Bloomberg).
GPU rental prices are rising: the median H100 price across 41 providers is US$3.57/hr, +7% over four weeks and +19% y/y.
Anthropic's Claude Haiku 5.5 launched at US$0.10/$0.50 per million tokens, 90% below Haiku 4.5. The price per token keeps collapsing.

sections.first_order: Hardware demand data (foundry, memory, GPU rental) still runs ahead of forecasts. The market is now questioning whether model-maker revenue can pay for it. SMH fell 6.8% on the week; QQQ fell only 1.3%.

second_order.effect: DRAM and HBM supply is tight, so memory pricing power continues (Samsung, SK Hynix, Micron)
Memory costs feed into device bills of materials. Apple reportedly cut iPhone component orders by at least 15%
AI-server demand lifted August electronics NODX by 131.8% y/y, which supports SG manufacturing and GDP
Rising GPU rents and lease rates (Applied Digital: more than 15% above prior contracts) support data-centre landlords and power demand, e.g. Keppel DC and Sembcorp
Circular financing (Broadcom→OpenAI, chip-backed loans) concentrates credit risk on ORCL, AMD and AVGO if OpenAI revenue disappoints

evidence: TSMC Q3 revenue beat the top of guidance; September sales +54.6% y/y (company release)
Samsung Q3 preliminary operating profit KRW107.4tn, above consensus; HBM bit shipments ~+50% q/q
H100 median rent +19% y/y: GPU compute is still scarce, not in glut
Last published 2026 capex guides: Alphabet US$195–205bn, Meta US$125–145bn
Against: OpenAI run-rate about US$50bn versus the market's ~US$70bn assumption; SMH -6.8% on the week
consensus: The OpenAI revenue gap is a test of the AI-infrastructure story; ORCL, AMD and AVGO are most exposed
Strength at Samsung and TSMC shows hardware demand is intact
Vendor financing is increasingly flagged as a circular-financing risk
Hyperscaler capex is expected to keep rising into 2027 on the Q3 calls
sections.flip_if: Any of these would flip the read: TSMC's 15 Oct call trims 2027 AI-accelerator growth or capex; a hyperscaler (Meta 21 Oct, MSFT/GOOGL 28 Oct) holds or cuts its capex guide; H100/B200 rental prices turn down; or OpenAI financing talks stall.

sections.headline: Bank-led STI correction: worst day since April 2025 as US yields hit 24-year highs

what_happened.text: STI fell 4.1% in the week to 9 Oct (5,635 → 5,401.89). The 8 Oct drop of 3.5% was the worst day since April 2025. The index is now below its 100-day average (~5,474) and about 7% off the 4 Sep intraday high of 5,828.50.
Citi cut OCBC to Sell (TP S$27.50) and kept UOB at Sell. OCBC fell 5.9% on the day. The three banks lost about S$22.4bn of market value in the week.
OCBC's dividend-yield spread over the 10-year SGS is about 70bp, near its lowest since 2010. ES3's forward P/E is 16.4x against a 12.3x average for 2021–26.
JPMorgan cut SGX to Neutral (TP S$23). The stock fell 7.2% on 2 Oct and is about 16% off its September high.
CICT and CLAR traded at or near 52-week lows on 13 Oct (S$2.21 and S$2.17).

sections.first_order: The selloff is about valuation and rates, not credit. Banks were priced at premium multiples with thin yield spreads, and rising US long yields brought in profit-taking. No bad-debt signal has appeared yet. REITs are grinding lower on rates.

second_order.effect: Higher-for-longer US yields keep REIT yields under pressure; CICT and CLAR are at 52-week lows ahead of their Q3 updates
Volatility lifts trading volumes, which partly offsets the derating
A ~S$22bn hit to bank market value and weaker portfolios soften discretionary big-ticket demand, including Cat B COE bids
ES3 has had 19 straight months of inflows (S$293m in Sep); a reversal would amplify the drawdown

evidence: STI closed below its 100-day average; 21-day RSI 34 (9 Oct)
ES3 forward P/E 16.4x vs 12.3x 2021–26 average; DBS at 2.87x book
OCBC dividend-yield spread over SGS 10y about 70bp, near its lowest since 2010
US 10y closed at 5.31% on 5 Oct (highest since 2002), 5.24% on 9 Oct
Against: banks' FY26 dividend yields 3.7–4.5%; no asset-quality deterioration reported; MAS tightening supports SGD assets
consensus: Citi: OCBC Sell (S$27.50), UOB Sell, DBS Buy
Jefferies: DBS Buy, UOB Buy, OCBC Hold; RHB overweight banks with OCBC its top pick
JPMorgan: higher long yields bring mark-to-market and deposit-cost pressure; OCBC most exposed
Julius Baer: no bad-debt signs, but expects more volatility in October
sections.flip_if: The read would flip if the US 10y falls back below ~5.0%, early-November bank Q3 results show stable NIMs and fee income, or the STI reclaims its 100-day average (~5,474) on breadth. A break below the 9 Oct low (5,369) would strengthen it.

sections.headline: LTA consults on merging Cat A and B; premiums ease a second round while buyers wait

what_happened.text: At the 7 Oct exercise Cat B closed at S$130,100 (-2.2%), its second straight fall from S$135,001 on 9 Sep, with 1.19 bids per COE. Cat A closed at S$130,001, now only S$99 below Cat B. Cat E was flat at S$137,000.

LTA opened a public consultation on merging Cat A and B into one car category, with a feebate banded by model OMV. Cat E may be removed or limited. Consultation closes 2 Nov; recommendations in 1H2027; no implementation date.
The EV Early Adoption Incentive ends 1 Jan 2027; maximum EV ARF savings fall from S$30k to S$20k in 2027.
The Aug–Oct 2026 quota was 19,085 (+0.2% q/q). LTA will announce the Nov 2026–Jan 2027 quota in October.

sections.first_order: Premiums are drifting lower on thin bid cover and a wait-and-see effect from the categorisation review. The end-2026 EEAI cut-off pulls EV demand forward into Nov–Dec, which works against further falls.

second_order.effect: Buyers deferring until the review outcome and the 24–25 Oct Car Expo slow order books near term; then a year-end rush before the EEAI expires
A merged category with OMV-banded feebates removes the advantage of EVs tuned to fit under the Cat A power limit; pull-forward helps near term
Gate 3 (Cat B < S$110k) is still a miss at S$130,100; direction is favourable but the step is small

evidence: Cat B down two rounds in a row: 135,001 → 133,000 → 130,100
Cat B bids per COE 1.19 (1,126 bids for 945 COEs) on 7 Oct
Cat A–B gap down to S$99, consistent with the policy-driven distortion LTA cites
EEAI ends 1 Jan 2027: a dated incentive for year-end EV demand
Nov–Jan quota not yet announced
consensus: Most dealers (Kah Motor, Eurokars, Motorway) expect premiums to stay flat or hover while buyers await the review
Some expect a dip at the 21 Oct round, then a rebound after the Car Expo
Motorist commentary predicts a peak in November 2026, then a dip
sections.flip_if: A bearish read needs the Nov–Jan quota (due ~23–24 Oct) to come in clearly above 19,085, or Cat B bid cover to fall below ~1.1. A bullish read needs a flat or lower quota plus a visible EEAI pull-forward in the 2 Nov and 18 Nov rounds.

sections.headline: Hormuz attacks put Brent back above US$106; refining margins near double for the majors

what_happened.text: Brent settled at US$106.65 on 12 Oct, the highest close since 15 Sep, up from US$100.20 on 7 Oct. WTI settled at US$93.25. Both eased ~1.9% on 13 Oct.
At least 12 tanker attacks hit ships in and around Hormuz from 28 Sep to 5 Oct, and UKMTO confirmed 6 strikes on 12 Oct. The IRGC calls the strait closed; the US says flows are near normal.
Qatar LNG remains under force majeure. Exports are forecast at ~0.6 Mt in October, down from 1.6 Mt in September.
Shell's Q3 update shows an indicative refining margin of US$42/bbl, up from US$24 in Q2. Its chemicals margin fell to US$208/t from US$270.
BP's Q3 trading statement puts realised refining margins US$1.9–2.1bn above Q2, with net debt falling to US$13.5–14.5bn.
OPEC+ kept November output unchanged on 4 Oct; next meeting 1 Nov. OPEC cut its 2026 demand-growth view to 0.4 mb/d.

sections.first_order: Supply risk is in the price and product cracks are exceptional, so Q3 earnings for integrated majors and refiners are set to step up. Upstream benefits from crude above US$100.

second_order.effect: Jet fuel tracks the diesel cracks. Higher fuel costs push fares up and weigh on price-sensitive travel demand (SIA, regional carriers)
Feedstock costs rise faster than product prices; Shell's chemicals margin fell from US$270/t to US$208/t
Qatar's outage keeps JKM at ~US$26/MMBtu, so oil- and LNG-indexed power costs in Japan, Korea and SG rise with a lag
Freight, fertiliser and packaging costs feed food prices; PepsiCo cut EPS guidance on input-cost inflation
The energy shock keeps inflation risks 'skewed to the upside' (FOMC minutes), so the Fed and MAS stay hawkish

evidence: Shell indicative refining margin US$42/bbl vs US$24 in Q2 (company update)
BP refining margins US$1.9–2.1bn stronger q/q (SEC 6-K)
Brent closes US$100.20 → US$106.65 over 7–12 Oct
Qatar LNG still under force majeure; JKM front-month US$25.98 on 9 Oct
XLE at US$66.01, near its 52-week high of 66.42
Against: OPEC demand-growth cut to 0.4 mb/d; US easing on Russian diesel; Fed hiking
consensus: Physical tightness keeps Brent above US$100 (SPI AM)
Russian diesel pledges unlikely to arrive in full (PVM)
The US midterms (3 Nov) are a binary point: escalation or a deal with Iran (Commerzbank)
sections.flip_if: A US–Iran deal or a verified reopening of Hormuz (the risk premium would collapse), Qatar lifting force majeure, or diesel cracks falling sharply before Q3 results (Shell 29 Oct, BP 30 Oct).

sections.headline: Q4 tariff cut is behind us; the fuel window for Q1 2027 is running at higher oil and LNG

what_happened.text: SP Group's Q4 2026 household tariff is 28.59 c/kWh (-10.4%), reflecting lower July–August fuel costs. City Energy gas is 21.45 c/kWh (-8.6%).
Keppel fell 4.81% to S$10.49 on 8 Oct on ~2x volume, with no named catalyst. That is a three-month low.
Brent is ~US$105–107 and JKM ~US$26/MMBtu in October, above the July–August levels that set the Q4 tariff.

sections.first_order: SG power is mostly gas-fired with oil-linked contracts, so the Q1 2027 tariff (set off fuel costs from about October to mid-December) points higher. Gencos pass this through, so the effect on their margins is mixed rather than a clear gain.

second_order.effect: A higher Q1 2027 tariff lifts headline CPI and the electricity gate of the Cat B thesis
Higher power and gas costs for hawkers, restaurants and supermarkets feed food-services inflation
An energy-led rise in core inflation supports continued S$NEER tightening
Power is a pass-through cost for DC operators, but higher tariffs squeeze tenants' total cost of ownership

evidence: Q4 tariff -10.4% set off lower Jul–Aug fuel costs (SP Group)
Brent and JKM are higher in the Q1 2027 fuel window than in Jul–Aug
Sembcorp at S$6.08 near the top of its recent range; Keppel at a three-month low
No material Sembcorp or Keppel announcements this week
consensus: Rystad expects a single-digit rise in the Q1 2027 tariff
Singapore International Energy Week (26–30 Oct) is expected to bring policy and LNG announcements
sections.flip_if: A sustained drop in oil below ~US$90 Brent before early December would cap the Q1 tariff rise. A Sembcorp or Keppel Q3 update showing margin compression or a strong renewables/DC contribution would sharpen the read either way.

sections.headline: Growth is price-led and input costs are rising again: PepsiCo cuts EPS guidance

what_happened.text: PepsiCo Q3 organic revenue +3.1%, of which about 3pts was pricing and ~0.5pt volume. FY26 core EPS guidance was cut to +2.5–3.5% on 'rising input cost inflation'.
FAO Food Price Index Sep 2026: 136.0 (+1.5% m/m, +5.8% y/y), the highest since Nov 2022. Sugar +6.1% and cereals +5.1% m/m; veg oils +18.3% y/y.
Costco September comps were +7.6% ex gas/FX (US +8.0%) and digital +19%. Value-focused retail is still taking share.
Nestlé guides 3–4% organic growth with volume (RIG) speeding up and pricing easing. Lower coffee and cocoa costs are partly offset by higher freight and energy costs from the Middle East conflict.

sections.first_order: Branded staples are leaning on price while volumes stay flat, and energy, freight and grain costs are turning up again. Margin guidance is the pressure point; scale discounters (Costco, Walmart) gain from trade-down.

second_order.effect: Trade-down and value-seeking keep Costco and Walmart traffic strong while branded makers lose pricing power
Higher cereal, sugar and veg-oil prices help processors and planters (e.g. Wilmar) but squeeze food manufacturers
Oil above US$100 raises resin and freight costs and passes them down the chain
Food and energy pass-through keeps headline CPI sticky, which supports hawkish central banks

evidence: PepsiCo FY26 core EPS guidance cut, citing input-cost inflation (8-K)
PepsiCo volume only ~+0.5pt of 3.1% organic growth
FAO FFPI 136.0, third straight monthly rise
Rising US long yields weigh on bond-proxy sectors; XLP 84.41 vs 52-week high 90.14
Against: Costco +7.6% comps; Nestlé guiding volume recovery; XLP has bounced since 1 Oct
consensus: PepsiCo's guidance cut is the template for P&G (22 Oct), Nestlé (22 Oct) and Unilever (28 Oct)
Nestlé is steering investors to slowing pricing and recovering volumes in H2
sections.flip_if: P&G or Nestlé (22 Oct) report volume recovery with stable gross margins and hold guidance; or oil and grains fall back, easing input costs; or US yields drop, which would re-rate defensives.

sections.headline: SG core inflation at a two-year high; Sheng Siong derated on valuation

what_happened.text: SG August CPI: headline 2.3%, MAS core 2.2% (highest since Sep 2024), with food a contributor.
Maybank cut Sheng Siong to Hold (TP S$3.12) on a 28.4x forward P/E and normalising growth. The stock fell 5.5% on 9 Oct.
DFI Retail is swapping its 50% stake in Maxim's for the Starbucks HK licence business plus ~US$340m cash. Its 2027 payout ratio rises to 80%.
Malaysian CPO futures eased to RM4,592 on 9 Oct after Budget 2027 left out an export-duty waiver.

sections.first_order: Grocers can pass through food inflation, so revenue holds up, but the sector re-rates on valuation. Wilmar is caught between firm grain and sugar prices and softer palm oil.

second_order.effect: Food inflation supports nominal sales; the JB–SG RTS Link (Jan 2027) risks cross-border grocery leakage
Higher ingredient, power and gas costs feed food-services prices
Rising core inflation strengthens the case for S$NEER tightening, and a stronger SGD damps imported-food costs

evidence: MAS core inflation 2.2% in August, a third straight rise
Sheng Siong at 28.4x forward P/E before the downgrade
Wilmar down from S$3.68 (25 Sep) to S$3.46; CPO softer
SG September CPI due ~23 Oct
consensus: Maybank: Sheng Siong Hold, TP S$3.12
Economists see core inflation drifting up on energy and food pass-through
sections.flip_if: SG September CPI (~23 Oct) shows food inflation rolling over, or CPO and grain prices fall sharply. A strong Sheng Siong Q3 would test the valuation derating.

sections.headline: Fed minutes: 'most' see another hike; ISM prices paid near 78 ahead of September CPI

what_happened.text: FOMC minutes (released 7 Oct): 'most participants' judged another hike 'likely appropriate by year end'. Inflation risks were 'skewed to the upside' from energy, AI investment and tariffs.
The 10-year Treasury closed at 5.31% on 5 Oct (highest since 2002), 5.24% on 9 Oct; the 2-year was 4.80%.
September payrolls +29k with July–August revised down 60k; unemployment 4.2%. Initial claims stay low at 197k.
Waller: more hikes are 'likely needed', but not necessarily at consecutive meetings.
ISM September: manufacturing 54.5 with prices 77.9; services 54.9 with prices 74.

sections.first_order: Policy is tightening into an energy shock while activity holds up (ISM above 54, low claims, HY spread 3.15%). Long yields sit at 24-year highs, and that is the common driver behind this week's equity, REIT and bank moves.

second_order.effect: Higher discount rates compress multiples; SG REITs are at 52-week lows
A steeper curve (10y–2y +0.44pp) helps NIMs, but mark-to-market losses and deposit competition offset it
Higher mortgage and car-loan rates weigh on big-ticket purchases, including SG floating-rate loans via SORA
Fed hikes support the USD; SGD is held up by MAS tightening

evidence: FOMC minutes: 'most' see another hike by year-end; inflation risks skewed up
ISM prices paid 77.9 (manufacturing) and 74 (services)
Brent above US$100 feeding headline CPI
Against: payrolls +29k with downward revisions; strong 10y auction; 10y eased ~7bp from its 5 Oct peak
consensus: US September CPI expected ~3.7% y/y headline, core ~2.4% (previews)
Markets price a 20–25% chance of an October hike and a year-end hike as the base case
sections.flip_if: A soft September CPI (14 Oct), a second weak payrolls print, or an IEA/OPEC-driven oil drop that lets the Fed skip December, which would pull the 10y back toward ~5.0%. The 27–28 Oct FOMC is the next test.

sections.headline: MAS decides 14 Oct: a third tightening is the base case as core inflation and exports run hot

what_happened.text: August NODX +46.2% y/y, with electronics +131.8%.
Q2 labour market: retrenchments rose to 4,620 (from 3,830); resident unemployment 2.9%; 1.48 vacancies per unemployed person.
DBS expects the MAS decision and Q3 advance GDP this week; StanChart calls a slight slope increase a 'close call'.
USD/SGD closed at 1.2793 on 12 Oct, in a tight 1.275–1.281 range since mid-September.

sections.first_order: Strong external demand and rising core inflation favour a firmer S$NEER slope. Retrenchments are edging up but from low levels.

second_order.effect: A stronger SGD trims margins for exporters outside electronics
A firmer SGD partly offsets USD-priced oil and food costs
SG rates (SGS 10y 2.45%) stay far below US rates, which cushions SG REIT funding costs relative to US peers
Rising retrenchments and an equity drawdown weigh on Cat B demand

evidence: MAS core inflation 2.2% (Aug), a third straight rise
NODX +46.2% y/y (Aug); PMI 51.7 (Sep)
Retrenchments 4,620 in Q2, up from 3,830
USD/SGD range-bound at 1.275–1.281; SGS 10y 2.448%
consensus: DBS, StanChart and CIMB expect +25bp of slope to ~1.5%; a hold is the main risk
DBS expects Q3 advance GDP of 5.4% y/y
CIMB targets USD/SGD 1.2620 by 30 Oct
sections.flip_if: If MAS holds on 14 Oct, the SGD weakens and the read turns more dovish. A Q3 GDP print well below ~5% or a jump in Q3 retrenchments would turn the read more bearish on SG growth.
